content: 1. Health workers from delivery, labor services, and neonatal intensive care units expressed varying levels of comfort and understanding regarding demand feeding. While demand feeding was generally accepted, some health workers felt insecure about promoting semi-demand or demand feeding practices. Older beliefs persisted in some cases, where providers continued to teach mothers to limit breastfeeding duration or wake infants every three hours. Providers were more comfortable with scheduled feeding than newer recommendations for demand feeding. 2. In India, a study revealed that only half of the interviewed nurses were aware of the concept of demand feeding. Another study in India found that most doctors and nurses preferred scheduled feeding, whereas auxiliary nurses and midwives favored demand feeding. In contrast, a study in Australia reported that demand feeding was encouraged as standard practice and integrated well into hospital routines, while scheduled feeding was limited to specialized areas with special care nurses. Similarly, in Canada, scheduled feeding practices were mostly confined to neonatal intensive care units and specialized areas, where strict documentation of feedings was required, making providers uncomfortable with demand feeding. 3. The evidence on demand feeding had low confidence due to minor methodological limitations, moderate concerns about coherence, and substantial concerns about relevance, as no studies were conducted in low-income countries. The data was considered fairly robust but not comprehensive. 4. Regarding early additional foods or fluids, health workers generally believed that breast milk was beneficial but also considered formula feeding acceptable. Several studies reported that health workers viewed infant formula as a safe option that would not harm the infant. Some studies indicated that health workers believed giving early additional foods or fluids was a mother’s choice, and formula should be an option if the mother desired it. One study found that only slightly more than half of health workers agreed that infants should not be supplemented unless medically indicated. Another study reported that most doctors occasionally recommended formula to breastfeeding mothers. Supplementation was not universally believed to harm breastfeeding, and some health workers viewed it as a way to protect mothers from nighttime fatigue or provide short-term relief. 5. In neonatal intensive care units, health workers described formula or fortified expressed breast milk as necessary for premature or ill infants. The evidence on this topic had moderate confidence, with minor methodological limitations, little inconsistency among studies, and moderate concerns about relevance and data adequacy. 6. Health workers had differing values regarding pacifier use. Some studies found mixed perceptions among health-care providers about advising women on pacifier use, with some finding it easy and others viewing it as an obstacle. There was an almost universal ambivalence among staff toward the use of teats and dummies. Some health workers felt that the practice of using or avoiding teats in hospitals was inconsistent and not open for discussion. The evidence had moderate confidence, with minor methodological limitations, little inconsistency, and moderate concerns about relevance and data adequacy. 7. Most health professionals disliked cup feeding and were ambivalent about bottle feeding. Some providers believed that the method of feeding made no difference and that bottle feeding might sometimes be better for the baby. Bottles were described as essential or beneficial when mothers were struggling. In India, half of the nurses believed that introducing a bottle in the first month of life was beneficial. One study described midwives’ perceptions that women who bottle-fed were closeted away because bottle feeding was discouraged in their facility. In neonatal intensive care units, bottles were considered necessary due to the prioritization of medical care over breastfeeding. Many studies reported that bottles were preferred by health-care providers over other feeding methods, such as cup feeding. 8. Health workers felt that implementing a breastfeeding policy was a daunting task requiring frequent communication. Maternity staff valued having a neutral breastfeeding policy, with the majority favoring a policy that did not emphasize one feeding method over another. However, some staff feared that having a policy might engender guilt among mothers who chose not to breastfeed or were unable to do so. Writing an infant feeding policy was seen as challenging, especially for administrators with no prior experience. Lack of resources to create and implement a policy was a barrier for hospital administration. Clear protocols and frequent communication were viewed as essential for establishing consistent breastfeeding messages. 9. Health workers felt that more breastfeeding training would be helpful, but competing priorities limited the time available for such training. Maternity staff welcomed breastfeeding training as a way to overcome negativity toward initiatives like the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative. However, most resident doctors found their breastfeeding education and training inadequate. Staff valued breastfeeding training but felt they lacked the time to complete it due to other educational priorities, such as training on skills to care for mothers with complications. Despite interest, breastfeeding education was often assigned a lower priority compared to other training needs. 10. Health workers had differing views on their roles in promoting breastfeeding during antenatal education. Many providers believed that promoting and supporting breastfeeding was part of their role. Some studies reported that providers felt counseling women on breastfeeding was an important use of their time during prenatal visits. However, there were variations in how providers approached their role in informing women about breastfeeding.
